products.name: Bananas, bunch of 5

specs.Storage: Keep at room temperature, away from other fruit

products.short: Five bananas picked green and ripened in our store, so they arrive yellow and keep for the week.
description: We buy our bananas green and ripen them ourselves, in small batches, so a bunch reaches you just turned yellow rather than already spotted. Leave them in the fruit bowl and they will see you through to the weekend.
Keep them away from apples and avocados if you want them to last: those give off the gas that ripens bananas faster.

products.name: Pink Lady apples, 6 pack

specs.Storage: Keep in the fridge for the longest crunch

products.short: Crisp, sweet-sharp apples, six to a bag, picked this autumn.
description: A crisp, juicy apple with a sweet-sharp bite. These come from an orchard two hours from the store and are picked when the blush has spread across the skin.
They keep for two weeks in the fridge, and slice into lunchboxes without browning too quickly.

products.name: Strawberries, 400 g

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated; eat within 2 days

products.short: Sweet British strawberries in a 400 g punnet, picked the day before delivery.
description: Picked in the morning, chilled straight away and with us the next day. That short trip is why they still taste of strawberries rather than of the fridge.
Take them out of the fridge half an hour before you eat them: they taste sweeter at room temperature.

products.name: Unwaxed lemons, 4 pack

specs.Storage: Keep in the fridge

products.short: Four unwaxed lemons, so the zest is ready to grate straight into cooking.
description: Unwaxed lemons are left as they come off the tree, which means you can zest them straight into a dressing, a cake or a pan of risotto without scrubbing first.
They keep for a fortnight in the fridge. Roll one on the worktop before squeezing to get more juice out of it.

products.name: Ripe and ready avocados, 2 pack

specs.Storage: Eat within 2 days, or keep in the fridge to slow ripening

products.short: Two avocados checked by hand for ripeness, ready to eat today or tomorrow.
description: Each avocado is pressed by hand before it is packed, so these are soft enough for toast the day they arrive.
Not eating them yet? Put them in the fridge, which slows ripening by a few days.

products.name: Vine tomatoes, 500 g

specs.Storage: Keep at room temperature for the best flavour

products.short: Glasshouse tomatoes ripened on the vine, sold on the stalk for flavour.
description: Grown in a glasshouse heated by its own solar panels and left on the vine until they are fully red. The stalk keeps feeding the fruit, which is why vine tomatoes taste sweeter.
Keep them out of the fridge: cold dulls the flavour. Slice them with a little salt and good olive oil and they hardly need anything else.

products.name: Carrots, 1 kg

specs.Storage: Keep in the fridge, out of the bag

products.short: A kilo of sweet, crunchy carrots from a farm near the store.
description: Washed but not peeled, so they keep their sweetness. Grated raw into a salad, roasted with honey or simmered into soup, a kilo bag goes a long way.
Take them out of the plastic and keep them in the fridge drawer: they stay crisp for up to two weeks.

products.name: Broccoli, 350 g

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated

products.short: A tight green head of broccoli, cut the day before it reaches you.
description: Look for a tight, dark green head: that is how ours arrive. Steam it for four minutes, or roast it hot with garlic and chilli until the edges crisp.
Do not throw the stalk away. Peeled and sliced, it is sweeter than the florets.

products.name: Mixed peppers, 3 pack

specs.Storage: Keep in the fridge

products.short: One red, one yellow and one green pepper for stir-fries, salads and traybakes.
description: Three colours, three slightly different flavours: green is grassy, yellow is mild and red is the sweetest of the three.
They keep for a week in the fridge. Roast them whole until black, peel, and keep them in olive oil for sandwiches.

products.name: Chestnut mushrooms, 250 g

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated in a paper bag

products.short: Firm brown mushrooms with more flavour than white ones, grown nearby.
description: Chestnut mushrooms are firmer and nuttier than white mushrooms and hold their shape in the pan. Fry them hot and do not crowd them, and they turn golden instead of watery.
Keep them in a paper bag in the fridge; plastic makes them sweat.

products.name: White sourdough loaf, 800 g

specs.Storage: Keep in a bread bag; freezes well sliced

products.short: A slow-proved sourdough with a dark crust, baked each morning by our partner bakery.
description: Made with flour, water, salt and a starter that is older than the bakery, then left to prove overnight. The long, slow rise gives the open crumb and the gentle sourness.
It keeps for four days in a bread bag. Slice what you will not eat and freeze it: it toasts straight from frozen.

products.name: All-butter croissants, 4 pack

specs.Storage: Best eaten on the day; warm for 3 minutes in the oven

products.short: Flaky croissants made with butter and nothing else, four to a bag.
description: Laminated by hand with proper butter and baked in the early hours. Warm them in a hot oven for three minutes and the layers crisp up again.
Day-old croissants make the best almond croissants or bread and butter pudding.

products.name: Stone-baked baguette, 250 g

specs.Storage: Best eaten on the day

products.short: A crackling stone-baked baguette with an airy crumb.
description: Baked on the oven floor for a crust that crackles when you squeeze it. Tear it while it is fresh; that is half the point of a baguette.
Left over? Slice it thinly, brush with olive oil and bake for crostini.

products.name: Cinnamon buns, 4 pack

specs.Storage: Best eaten within 2 days

products.short: Soft, cardamom-scented cinnamon buns, baked on Fridays and Saturdays.
description: A soft enriched dough rolled with cinnamon butter and a little cardamom, then glazed with syrup as it comes out of the oven.
Baked on Fridays and Saturdays only, so they sell out. Check back at the weekend.

products.name: Free-range eggs, 12 pack

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated

products.short: A dozen free-range eggs from hens that roam an orchard twenty miles away.
description: From a small flock that spends its days outside in an old orchard. The eggs are mixed in size, which is how hens lay them, and collected the morning before they are packed.
Store them pointed end down in the fridge, and bring them to room temperature before baking.

products.name: Whole milk, 2 litres

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated; use within 3 days of opening

products.short: Creamy whole milk from one dairy farm, bottled within a day of milking.
description: All of our milk comes from one family farm, so it tastes the same from one week to the next. It is pasteurised but not homogenised, so a little cream rises to the top: give it a shake.
Two litres covers most households for three or four days of tea, coffee and cereal.

products.name: Greek-style yogurt, 500 g

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated; eat within 5 days of opening

products.short: Thick, strained yogurt with a gentle tang, for breakfast bowls and marinades.
description: Strained until it is thick enough to stand a spoon in. Spoon it over fruit and oats, stir it into curries at the end of cooking, or use it to marinate chicken.
Five hundred grams is a week of breakfasts for one, or a generous bowl of tzatziki.

products.name: Mature cheddar, 400 g

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated, wrapped

products.short: A sharp, crumbly cheddar aged for twelve months.
description: Aged for a year, which gives it the savoury crunch of little crystals and a sharp finish. Good on its own with an apple, and better still grated over pasta.
Wrap it in wax paper rather than cling film, and take it out of the fridge an hour before serving.

products.name: Salted butter, 250 g

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated

products.short: Rich, lightly salted butter churned from grass-fed cream.
description: Churned from the cream of grass-fed cows, which is what gives it the deep yellow colour. Lightly salted, for toast, baking and finishing sauces.
Keep a little out of the fridge in a butter dish so it spreads.

products.name: Basmati rice, 1 kg

specs.Storage: Keep in a cool, dry place

products.short: Aged long-grain basmati that cooks up fluffy and fragrant.
description: Aged for a year before milling, which makes the grains longer and less sticky once cooked. Rinse it until the water runs clear, then cook one cup of rice to one and a half of water.
A kilo bag makes about twelve generous portions.

products.name: Penne pasta, 500 g

specs.Storage: Keep in a cool, dry place

products.short: Bronze-cut penne with a rough surface that holds on to sauce.
description: Pushed through bronze dies and dried slowly, which leaves a rough surface that sauce clings to. Cook it in plenty of well-salted water for eleven minutes.
Save a mug of the cooking water before you drain it: a splash loosens any sauce.

products.name: Red split lentils, 1 kg

specs.Storage: Keep in a cool, dry place

products.short: Organic red lentils that cook down in fifteen minutes, no soaking.
description: Split red lentils need no soaking and collapse into a creamy dal or soup in about fifteen minutes. They are one of the cheapest sources of protein in the store.
Rinse them first, and cook with three times their volume of water or stock.

products.name: Extra virgin olive oil, 500 ml

specs.Storage: Keep in a cool, dark cupboard

products.short: A green, peppery extra virgin olive oil from a single Greek estate.
description: Pressed within hours of picking, from olives grown on one estate. It is grassy and peppery, with the little catch at the back of the throat that good fresh oil has.
Use it for finishing: over tomatoes, soups and bread. Keep it away from the hob, as heat and light dull the flavour.

products.name: Wildflower honey, 340 g

specs.Storage: Keep at room temperature

products.short: Runny honey from hives kept on meadows near the store.
description: From a beekeeper who keeps her hives on wildflower meadows, so the flavour changes a little with each harvest. It is gently warmed to jar it, never heated.
If it sets, stand the jar in warm water for ten minutes.

products.name: Rolled oats, 1 kg

specs.Storage: Keep in a cool, dry place

products.short: Organic jumbo oats for porridge, overnight oats and flapjacks.
description: Big, whole rolled oats that keep some bite in porridge and soak up milk overnight without turning to mush.
A kilo bag makes about twenty bowls of porridge. Toast a handful in a dry pan to sprinkle over yogurt.

products.name: Medium roast coffee beans

specs.Storage: Keep sealed, away from light

products.short: A smooth, chocolatey everyday roast, roasted in small batches every week.
description: Roasted every Tuesday by a small roaster across town, and dated on the bag. It is a medium roast with notes of cocoa and toasted hazelnut, and it works in a cafetiere, a filter or an espresso machine.
Buy the bag you will finish in three weeks: that is how long beans stay at their best once opened. The kilo bag has the lowest price per kilo.

products.name: English breakfast tea, 80 bags

specs.Storage: Keep dry, away from strong smells

products.short: A strong, malty breakfast blend in plastic-free bags.
description: A blend of Assam and Kenyan teas that stands up to milk. Brew for four minutes for a proper cup.
The bags are made from plant fibre with no plastic, so they can go in the food waste.

products.name: Orange juice, not from concentrate, 1 litre

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated; use within 4 days of opening

products.short: Pressed oranges and nothing else, with plenty of bits.
description: Squeezed from Spanish oranges and gently pasteurised, never made from concentrate. It has plenty of bits, the way fresh juice does.
Shake before pouring: the pulp settles.

products.name: Cloudy lemonade, 1 litre

specs.Storage: Keep refrigerated after opening

products.short: A sharp, still cloudy lemonade made with pressed lemons.
description: Made with pressed lemon juice, cane sugar and water, so it is properly sharp. Serve it over ice with a sprig of mint.
Mix half and half with sparkling water for a lighter drink.

products.name: Dark chocolate 70%, 100 g

specs.Storage: Keep cool and dry

products.short: A smooth 70% dark chocolate with notes of red fruit.
description: Made from a single origin cocoa with red fruit notes and a smooth finish, sweet enough to eat by the square and dark enough to bake with.
Keep it somewhere cool but not in the fridge, where it can bloom.

products.name: Mixed nuts, 200 g

specs.Storage: Keep sealed after opening

products.short: Unsalted almonds, cashews, hazelnuts and walnuts.
description: A plain mix of four nuts with nothing added: no salt, no oil. Toast them in a dry pan for a couple of minutes to bring out the flavour.
Allergy advice: contains nuts, and is packed where peanuts are handled.

products.name: Oat and raisin cookies, 200 g

specs.Storage: Keep in an airtight tin

products.short: Chewy oat and raisin cookies, baked with butter.
description: Chewy in the middle and crisp at the edges, with plump raisins and a pinch of cinnamon. Made by the same bakery as our bread.
Keep them in a tin and they stay chewy for a week.

products.name: Dried apricots, 250 g

specs.Storage: Keep sealed in a cool, dry place

products.short: Soft, sweet dried apricots with no added sugar.
description: Sun-dried and left soft, with no added sugar. Chop them into porridge, tagines and flapjacks, or eat them straight from the bag.
They are unsulphured, so they are brown rather than bright orange. That is how apricots look when they dry naturally.

products.name: Tulips, bunch of 10

specs.Care: Trim the stems and change the water every two days

products.short: Ten tulips in bud, so they open in your vase rather than in the van.
description: Cut in tight bud, so they open over a few days at home. Tulips keep growing in the vase, so give them a tall one and expect them to bend towards the light.
Trim the stems at an angle and change the water every couple of days.

products.name: Hand-dipped beeswax candles, 2 pack

specs.Care: Trim the wick to 5 mm before lighting

products.short: Two hand-dipped beeswax candles that burn slowly with a faint smell of honey.
description: Dipped by hand, one layer at a time, from the wax of the same hives that make our honey. Beeswax burns slower and cleaner than paraffin and smells faintly of honey as it does.
Trim the wick before lighting and keep them out of draughts, and each one lasts about eight hours.

products.name: Olive oil soap, 4 x 100 g
products.short: Four bars of plain, unscented olive oil soap, gentle enough for hands and face.
description: Made the traditional way, with olive oil and nothing to scent or colour it. It lathers gently and suits sensitive skin.
Let it dry between uses on a draining soap dish and each bar lasts for weeks.

products.name: Wooden dish brush

specs.Care: Rinse and leave to dry head down

products.short: A beech dish brush with stiff plant-fibre bristles. No plastic.
description: A solid beech handle and stiff plant-fibre bristles that get into the corners of pans. When the bristles wear out, the handle can go on the compost.
Leave it to dry head down so the wood does not stay wet.

bananas: Ripe on arrival and they lasted the whole week. Exactly what I want from bananas.
Good bunch. One was a little greener than the rest, which suited me fine.
free-range-eggs: Big eggs with deep orange yolks, and not one cracked in the box.
The best eggs we have had from any delivery. We order a dozen every week now.
sourdough-loaf: A proper crust and a chewy crumb. It still toasts beautifully on day four.
Lovely bread. I would buy a smaller loaf too if you made one.
It arrived still smelling of the oven.
vine-tomatoes: They actually taste of tomato. Great sliced with salt and olive oil.
extra-virgin-olive-oil: Peppery and fresh. The price per litre on the label made it easy to see it beats the supermarket.
Very good oil. I just wish there was a bigger bottle.
coffee-beans: Smooth and chocolatey, no bitterness at all. The kilo bag works out cheapest.
Fresh beans with the roast date on the bag. I order every two weeks.
strawberries: Sweet and well packed. A couple were soft by day three, so eat them quickly.
whole-milk: Creamy and it arrives properly cold. The cream on top is a nice surprise.
mature-cheddar: Sharp and crumbly with those little crystals. Just how cheddar should be.
dark-chocolate: Rich without being bitter. One square after dinner is enough.
greek-style-yogurt: Thick and creamy. Perfect with honey and oats.
rolled-oats: They make the best porridge, and a kilo bag is very good value.
all-butter-croissants: Flaky and buttery. Three minutes in the oven and they are as good as a bakery.

content: Every offer shows what you save and, where it has one, the day it ends. Prices on the tickets already include the discount: there is nothing to apply at checkout.

content.heading: A corner shop that happens to deliver
content.text: Good food, fairly priced, and honest about both.

items: eBasket started with one van, a handful of growers and a list of what our neighbours bought every week. The list grew into a store and the van into a small fleet, but the idea stayed the same: buy close to home, price it fairly, and tell people exactly what they are paying for.
That is why every shelf ticket shows the price per kilo, per litre or per item, and why every offer says when it ends. We would rather you compared us properly than took our word for it.

items.heading: Grown nearby, on the shelf by morning
items.text: Buying from farms close to the store means produce spends a night in a van instead of a week in a warehouse. It tastes better, and it wastes less.
The unit prices on every product make the weekly shop so much quicker to compare.

delivery.title: Delivery and collection
content: Choose delivery or collection at checkout. Chilled and frozen food travels in insulated boxes, and you can change your order until we start packing it.
Click and collect from the store: free.
We deliver every day between 7:00 and 22:00. Pick a one-hour window after you order and we will send a text when the van is on its way.
Can I change my order after checkout?
Yes. Add or remove items from your account until we start packing, usually two hours before your slot.
What happens if something is out of stock?
We suggest the closest match and only send it if you allowed swaps for that item. Otherwise it comes off the bill.
Do I need to be home?
For chilled and frozen food, yes. Leave a note at checkout if a neighbour can take it in for you.

faq.title: Help and FAQs
content: The questions we are asked most, with straight answers. Anything else, get in touch and a person will reply.
No. Small baskets pay the delivery fee; baskets over £40 are delivered free.
Every shelf ticket shows the pack size and the price per kilo, per litre or per item, so a big pack and a small one are easy to compare.
When you place the order. If anything is missing or swapped, the difference is refunded to your card.
Something was not fresh. What now?
Tell us within 24 hours of delivery from your orders page and the item is refunded. There is no need to send it back.

contact.title: Contact us
content: The quickest way to sort out an order is from your orders page, where every order has a Help button. For anything else, write to us or come and see us.

freshness-promise.title: Freshness promise and refunds
content: If anything you buy from us is not as fresh as it should be, we refund it. That is the whole promise.
Open your orders page within 24 hours of delivery.
Choose the order and press Help next to the item.
Tell us what was wrong. The refund goes back to your card within three working days.
Food cannot be resold, so there is no need to send it back. Unopened household items can be returned within 30 days for a full refund.

tomato-and-basil-penne.title: Tomato and basil penne in twenty minutes
tomato-and-basil-penne.excerpt: Ripe vine tomatoes melted into good olive oil: a weeknight pasta that tastes of more than its five ingredients.
content: The trick with a quick tomato sauce is ripe tomatoes and more olive oil than feels reasonable. Cook the tomatoes until they collapse, and the oil and juice turn into a glossy sauce in the time the pasta takes to boil.
Bring a large pan of well-salted water to the boil and cook the penne for 11 minutes.
Meanwhile warm the olive oil in a frying pan over a medium heat and add the garlic. Cook for a minute without letting it brown.
Add the tomatoes and a good pinch of salt. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, pressing them with a spoon, until they collapse into a sauce.
Scoop a mug of the pasta water, then drain the penne and tip it into the sauce with a splash of the water. Toss for a minute until glossy.
Tear in the basil, season with pepper and serve with the cheddar on top.
Everything except the basil and garlic is in the Pantry, Vegetables and Dairy aisles.

overnight-oats-three-ways.title: Overnight oats, three ways
overnight-oats-three-ways.excerpt: Five minutes the night before, and breakfast is waiting in the fridge. One base, three toppings for the week.
content: Overnight oats are the breakfast for people who do not have time for breakfast. Stir oats into milk and yogurt before bed, and by morning they have soaked into something thick and creamy.
For one jar: 50 g rolled oats, 100 ml whole milk, 2 tablespoons Greek-style yogurt and a teaspoon of honey. Stir, cover and leave in the fridge overnight.
Strawberries and honey: sliced strawberries and an extra drizzle of honey.
Banana and chocolate: sliced banana and a square of dark chocolate, grated.
Apricot and nut: chopped dried apricots and a handful of toasted mixed nuts.
The jars keep for three days in the fridge, so make a few at once.

a-proper-weekday-salad.title: A weekday salad that is actually filling
a-proper-weekday-salad.excerpt: Lentils, roasted peppers and a sharp lemon dressing: a salad that keeps you going until dinner.
content: A salad that keeps you full needs something substantial in it. Red lentils cook in fifteen minutes and soak up a dressing beautifully.
1 tablespoon olive oil, plus 3 for the dressing
Juice and zest of 1 unwaxed lemon
Roast the peppers with a tablespoon of oil at 200 °C for 20 minutes.
Simmer the lentils in plenty of water for 12 to 15 minutes, until just tender, then drain.
Whisk the lemon juice and zest with the rest of the oil and season well.
Toss the warm lentils with the dressing, then fold in the peppers and leaves.
It keeps in the fridge for two days, so it travels well as a packed lunch.
